findings.claim: The write-access trust filter only covers claims, revocations and handoffs. Everything else agents act on in a public GitHub tracker issue has no actor filter: scope, brief and decision comments, body edits, close/reopen, labels and assignees. On a public repo, a non-collaborator can still inject scope, and anyone who can close or label the issue can change its derived state.
findings.evidence: coordination.md lines 11-13: "Claims, revocations and handoffs count only from accounts with write access". workflow.md step 1 makes agents fetch "its description, comments, status and relations" and reconcile them, and line 58 sends "Linear scope ... comment" duties to the tracker issue. The repo is public (gh api repos/gyldlab/keld shows visibility public). The body of tracker issue #520 says "The authoritative agent contract is the latest **Agent Brief** comment on this issue", and any GitHub user can post a later "Agent Brief" comment. The state mapping (closed as completed = Done, closed as not planned = Canceled, ready-for-agent label = Todo) reads fields that the issue author can set by closing their own issue, and that triage-role users can set. The permission API reports triage as "read", so those same actors are untrusted for claims.
findings.fix: In coordination.md § GitHub tracker issue, apply the filter to every input agents rely on. Count only comments, body edits and state, label and assignee events from write-access accounts, checked through the issue timeline/events actor. Treat any other actor's change to scope, brief, state or labels as a conflict to report, never as input. Require the tracker issue itself to be authored or last edited by a write-access account.

refute.reasoning: I reproduced the finding independently. Before this change the tracker was the private Linear workspace, so every comment and state change came from a workspace member. This change makes a public GitHub issue the tracker of record. In workflow.md § Tracker issue it sends all "Linear scope, claim, status, comment and handoff duties" to that issue. Loop step 1 still tells agents to fetch "its description, comments, status and relations" and reconcile them. But the only actor filter added in coordination.md § GitHub tracker issue covers "Claims, revocations and handoffs". Nothing filters scope, brief or decision comments, which any GitHub user can post on a public issue. Nothing filters the state inputs either. The state mapping reads close reason, the `ready-for-agent` label and the assignee, and two kinds of actor the claim filter does not trust can set them: the issue author can close their own issue, and triage users can close, label and assign. That second kind exists today. gyldlab/keld has a triage collaborator, `keldrobo`, and the permission endpoint named in the rule returns `permission: read` for it. So the rule treats that account as untrusted for claims, yet its actions still decide Done, Canceled, Todo and In Progress. No other repo instruction makes issue comments untrusted: the untrusted-input rules in the autofix and code-review skills cover only PR review output, and memory.md covers only recalled memory. The finding is slightly overstated in one place. Body edits are limited to the author and triage-or-higher users, and the Linear back-link partly anchors who created the tracker issue. findings.claim: workflow.md and coordination.md give two different ordering keys for GitHub claims. workflow.md orders by creation time; coordination.md says an edited claim counts from its last edit. Under the edit rule, an owner who refreshes its winning claim by editing it, as the refresh rules invite, drops behind any competing claim posted in the meantime, and ownership flips.
findings.evidence: workflow.md lines 59-60: "Claims post and order only there, by its own creation timestamps". coordination.md lines 12-13: "an edited claim counts from its last edit". workflow.md lines 191 and 198-199 require refreshing the claim ("refreshing while actually working", "The claim MUST be refreshed at each substantial milestone") and never say a refresh must be a new comment. #520's proposed text also says "the earliest claim by GitHub's comment `created_at` wins". Scenario: agent A claims at t1. Agent B posts a claim at t2, sees A's unexpired claim and stops, but B's claim comment stays. A edits its claim at t3 to refresh the expiry. By coordination.md, B's claim is now the earliest, so A must stop at its next re-fetch while B was told not to begin.
findings.fix: Use one ordering key. In coordination.md, say claims order by comment `created_at` (matching workflow.md and #520). Refreshes are new claim comments that keep the original's priority. An edit to a claim comment after a competing claim exists voids that claim and is a conflict; it is never re-timestamped. Alternatively, change workflow.md to the same rule, but the two files must not disagree.

refute.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding; I reproduced it from the branch text. This branch's only commit (e972271b) adds both rules, and they give different ordering keys. workflow.md § Tracker issue says claims "post and order only there, by its own creation timestamps", and step 1 says "The earliest claim by Linear's own `createdAt` wins". The new GitHub section in coordination.md says "an edited claim counts from its last edit". Both are new in this diff, so the conflict comes from this change and was not there before.

Nothing in the text closes the gap. workflow.md lines 191-192 and 198-199 require the claim to be refreshed ("refreshing while actually working", "MUST be refreshed at each substantial milestone"). Neither file says a refresh must be a new comment rather than an edit to the existing claim. Neither file requires a claimant that lost and stopped to withdraw or delete its claim comment. The only "release the claim" text (coordination.md:110) applies when work is Done.

So the scenario holds as written. A claims at t1. B claims at t2, sees A's earlier claim and stops, and B's comment stays. A refreshes by editing its claim at t3. Under coordination.md, A's claim now counts from t3, so B's t2 claim is the earliest and wins, even though B was told to stop. If A refreshed with a new comment instead, A's original t1 claim would still exist and A would keep winning. That makes the result depend on how A refreshes, which the docs never specify. The "last edit" rule probably exists so nobody can backdate a claim by editing an old comment. That purpose is reasonable, but it does not remove the contradiction or the flip.

findings.claim: The first-match state mapping has no rule for issues closed as duplicate. Because the In Progress, Todo and Blocked clauses do not require the issue to be open, a closed duplicate can resolve to Todo (and be picked up), to In Progress, or to Blocked.
